question: The successive waves of bird flu have not only resulted in the regular slaughtering of all poultry on affected farms, but also in all previously free-range poultry having to be kept in claustration. This is bad both for animal welfare and consumers, as meat is labelled ‘free-range’ despite the poultry having been reared indoors.

France, however, is going to test biosecurity measures against bird and swine flu specifically designed for independent open-air farms across dozens of holdings. The aim is to eventually get open-air farms back up and running, for the good of animals and consumers. 1.
Does the Commission know whether similar tests are being carried out in other EU Member States?
Would it be ready to fund further tests to this end?

As poultry vaccination has not proven to be effective, would it not be better to favour independent open-air farms, without systematic slaughtering, to allow for the selection of poultry that are more resistant to bird flu?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.3.2024) The Commission is not aware of studies being carried out by Member States to test biosecurity measures in open-air farms to protect against influenza viruses. The consecutive framework programmes for Research and Innovation Horizon 20201 and Horizon Europe2 have consistently funded research on farm biosecurity3.

The forthcoming European Partnership on animal health and welfare4 will also prioritise biosecurity measures from its inception. According to Regulation (EU) 2016/4295, operators are responsible for the health of the animals they keep and reducing the risk of the spread of diseases.

They must implement suitable biosecurity measures tailored to the species and categories of kept animals and risks involved, including biosecurity measures regarding wild animals. Highly pathogenic avian influenza is categorized by the EU legislation6 as a category A disease for which immediate eradication measures must be taken as soon as it is detected.

Therefore, when detected in kept birds, regardless of the biosecurity measures in the establishment or the vaccination status, all eradication measures must be taken, including culling of all birds in the outbreak.

Under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)7, funding is available through the European Innovation Partnership (EIP-AGRI) for cooperation projects8 to test innovative farming practices, including measures for animal welfare and biosecurity. In addition, the French CAP Strategic Plan9 promotes diversification of practices and productions to foster risk prevention and resilience in production systems.
It emphasizes support for investment in preventive health measures, including biosecurity.
